summary.text: New Horizons is a NASA interplanetary space probe launched in 2006 as part of the New Frontiers program.
It was the first spacecraft to fly past Pluto and its moons and take high-resolution photographs of them, passing 12,500 km above Pluto's surface on July 14, 2015.
After Pluto it flew by the Kuiper belt object Arrokoth on January 1, 2019, and as of April 2026 it is traveling through the Kuiper belt.

facts.label: Launched
facts.value: January 19, 2006, on an Atlas V rocket

facts.label: Launch speed
facts.value: About 16.26 km/s relative to the Sun

items.prompt: New Horizons was headed for Pluto but passed close to giant Jupiter first. What did the pass do for it?

options.label: Jupiter's gravity gave it a speed boost
It slowed the probe for a gentler Pluto approach
It refilled the probe's thrusters with fuel
It let the probe drop a lander onto Jupiter

items.explain: The Jupiter flyby provided a gravity assist that increased New Horizons' speed.

items.prompt: New Horizons spent most of the trip after Jupiter switched mostly off, waking only briefly each year. What was the reason?

options.label: Its instruments broke at Jupiter and could not be used
To preserve its onboard systems
Ground controllers had lost contact with it
Pluto's gravity needed the probe to be asleep

items.explain: Most of the post-Jupiter voyage was spent in hibernation mode to preserve onboard systems, apart from brief annual checkouts.

items.prompt: Which statement about New Horizons' speed is accurate?

options.label: It holds the top recorded speed of any spacecraft as of 2026
Parker Solar Probe was launched from Earth faster than it
Fastest ever launched from Earth, but Parker Solar Probe holds the top recorded speed
Fastest ever launched, and no spacecraft has gone faster since

items.explain: New Horizons was the fastest human-made object ever launched from Earth, but the fastest speed recorded for a spacecraft is that of the Parker Solar Probe.

items.prompt: NASA's budget for 2003 left New Horizons out. What helped the mission win funding?

options.label: Congress overruled NASA's Administrator with a vote
Pluto's discoverer paid for it himself
It merged with the rival Pluto mission concept
The scientific community ranked it highest in its size category

items.explain: After Stern lobbied, the Decadal Survey placed New Horizons at the top of the medium-size projects, and funding was secured after the report came out.

items.prompt: Having finished with Pluto, what did New Horizons do next?

options.label: It maneuvered to fly past the Kuiper belt object Arrokoth
It entered orbit around Pluto for long study
It turned back toward Earth
It landed on Arrokoth

items.explain: After Pluto, New Horizons maneuvered for a flyby of Arrokoth.

items.prompt: NASA plans to extend operations for New Horizons until which event happens?

options.label: It reaches the orbit of Jupiter again
The spacecraft exits the Kuiper belt
It completes a second Pluto flyby
It catches up with the Voyager probes

items.explain: NASA plans to keep operating the mission until the spacecraft exits the Kuiper belt.

paragraphs.heading: The probe that went to Pluto
paragraphs.text: New Horizons is a NASA space probe sent out under the New Frontiers program. It launched in 2006 and became the first spacecraft to fly past Pluto and its moons and photograph them in high resolution. Engineers at the Southwest Research Institute and at the Johns Hopkins University Applied Physics Laboratory (APL) designed it. Alan Stern led the team.

paragraphs.heading: A fast start
paragraphs.text: It left Cape Canaveral on January 19, 2006, on an Atlas V rocket, aimed straight onto a path that would carry it away from both Earth and the Sun. Measured by average speed relative to Earth, it was the fastest object people had ever launched from Earth. The Parker Solar Probe, though, holds the record for top spacecraft speed. On February 28, 2007 New Horizons passed Jupiter at a distance of 2.3 million kilometers. Jupiter's gravity sped it up, and the flyby also tested its instruments, returning data on the planet's atmosphere, moons and magnetosphere.

paragraphs.heading: A long sleep
paragraphs.text: For most of the trip after Jupiter the probe hibernated to protect its systems, waking only for short yearly checkouts. On December 6, 2014, the team brought it back online and began checking its instruments. The approach to Pluto started on January 15, 2015.

paragraphs.heading: Pluto at last
paragraphs.text: On July 14, 2015, New Horizons flew 12,500 km above the surface of Pluto. It was the first spacecraft to explore the dwarf planet. The last of the data from the Pluto flyby reached Earth on October 25, 2016.

paragraphs.heading: Into the Kuiper belt
paragraphs.text: After Pluto, the team steered the probe toward Arrokoth, an object in the Kuiper belt then nicknamed Ultima Thule. It flew past on January 1, 2019, about 6.49 billion km from the Sun. It is still crossing the Kuiper belt, and in April 2026 it was about 9.64 billion km from the Sun. NASA plans to keep it running until it leaves the Kuiper belt, which is expected in 2028 or 2029.

paragraphs.heading: The mission that nearly wasn't
paragraphs.text: New Horizons was chosen for funding in November 2001. Then NASA's new administrator, Sean O'Keefe, left it out of the 2003 budget, which in effect canceled it. After a hard campaign for support, the Planetary Science Decadal Survey came out in summer 2002. This ranked wish list from the scientific community put New Horizons at the top of the medium-size missions, ahead of missions to the Moon and to Jupiter. Once the report was out, the money was finally secured.
